prose:
Lu Zhen prepared for the year-end Zhu Fu festival, the great rite that welcomed the gods of fortune and begged for the coming year's blessings. Along the canals of the closed Zhejiang water town, chickens were slaughtered, geese wrung, and pork bought in great slabs. Women plunged their arms into wooden basins, scrubbing the meat until their skin turned raw and red. The air smelled of blood and wine and the sharp incense burning in ancestral halls.

The town was ruled by landlords and gentry, its rigid order anchored by the study of Fourth Master Lu, a scholar of Neo-Confucianism and a former Imperial College student. He kept a library of moral treatises and frowned at anything that disturbed the ancient proprieties. In his household, as in all others, the clan system held absolute sway. A woman belonged first to her father, then to her husband, and finally to her son. If she lost all three, she belonged to no one but the charity of others.

Among the servants who scrubbed the festival meat was a woman known only as Xianglin's wife. Her given name had never been recorded, and no one thought to ask. She had been wife to Xianglin, who died in the spring of their first marriage. Then her mother-in-law had sold her to a man deep in the mountains, binding her with ropes and forcing a second union. She had fought so hard she split her head against the bed frame, but in the end she was made to go. That second husband died of typhoid, and her little boy, Ah Mao, was taken by a wolf while watching beans in the field. That, too, happened in spring.

Fourth Master Lu frowned when she came back to his compound. She was unclean, he said, a widow who had remarried, defiled by her own survival. During the Zhu Fu ceremony she was not permitted to touch the cups, the chopsticks, or the candles. The women averted their eyes. The men looked through her. She was a thing that had been used and broken.

She heard that a threshold donated to the Earthly God Temple could cleanse her sin. The price was twelve silver dollars—more than she could earn in a year. She saved every coin, hiding them in a cloth, never spending a cent for herself. When at last she carried the money to the temple, the priest shook his head. She wept until he relented. The threshold was purchased and laid before the inner shrine.

She knelt on it for a long time, believing she had bought her way back into the world of the clean.

But when the next festival came, she was still forbidden to touch the offerings. The ritual of blessings went on without her, as it always had, in a town that knew her only by a dead man's name.
